title: The first battle

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vibhishana crosses, the brother who told the truth twice and then walked over. Your line was walk across. Did you say one true thing? Day sixty-one.

Some nights the noise doesn't stop. The neighbors are fighting, the baby won't sleep, your phone keeps lighting up, your own head won't quiet down. Now picture Lanka. A golden city on a mountain, ringed with walls and moats, four great gates, each one guarded by an army. And outside, on the plain, a sea of monkeys and bears, and two princes with bows. The talking is over. Angada's embassy failed. Vibhishana has told Rama where every gate is. At dawn, the monkeys rush the walls, climbing, hurling rocks and trees. And the fighting doesn't stop when the sun goes down.
screen: `THE GOLDEN CITY, WALLED.` → `FOUR GATES, FOUR ARMIES.` → `THE MONKEYS RUSH THE WALLS.`

segments.voice: Valmiki's war books are long, loud and crowded. Hundreds of verses of duels: monkey against demon, one champion against another, names you'll never need to remember. And the first day's fighting runs into the night. That's when it gets frightening. The demons of Lanka are said to grow stronger in the dark. Nobody can see who's friend and who's enemy. Valmiki describes the night battle as a terrible darkness filled with shouting, the clash of weapons, cries in the dark, rivers of blood. The monkeys lash out at shadows. Some of them fight their own side by mistake. It's chaos. And in the middle of it, the story keeps putting one image in front of us: Rama, steady. Arrows coming from every side, and he answers them calmly, one at a time, as if the noise isn't touching him. That's the thing the story knows. A battle isn't only outside. The noise gets in. The fear gets in. The confusion gets in. You start swinging at shadows. The Gita, which we'll open in a later camp, has a word for the person who stays level in pleasure and pain, in noise and quiet: sthitaprajna, the one whose wisdom stands still. Rama, in this scene, is a picture of that. Not someone who's escaped the fight. Someone who's in the middle of it, still inside. The walls of Lanka won't fall for a long time. This is the first night of many. And already the question is not only who wins, but who can stay steady until morning.
screen: `THE FIGHTING RUNS INTO THE NIGHT.` · `IN THE DARK, SWINGING AT SHADOWS.` · `RAMA, STEADY, ONE ARROW AT A TIME.` · `STHITAPRAJNA: WISDOM THAT STANDS STILL.`

segments.voice: Sit where you are, and don't try to make it quiet. Whatever noise is around you, traffic, voices, a hum, a fan, let it be there. Now notice your breath underneath it. The noise is outside; the breath is inside. Every time a sound grabs you, notice it, then come back to one breath. If your mind is the noisy one, same thing: notice the thought, come back to the breath. You're not winning against the noise. You're just staying level in it. The bell holds the time.
The first battle. Lanka's walls, the fighting that runs into the dark, and one warrior who stays steady inside it.
Your line: still, inside. Today, when things get loud, take one breath before you swing at anything. Day sixty-one.

howItsDone: The war in Lanka is staged over several nights in the Ramlila plays of north India that lead up to Dussehra; many Hindus read the battle both as a story and as a picture of the inner struggle to stay steady.

fork.setup: you're in the night battle. it's pitch dark, shouting everywhere, and something moves beside you. what do you do?
options: stop, and look before you strike.
fork.reveal: in the story, the monkeys who swung at shadows sometimes hit their own side. the image the story holds up instead is Rama, steady, one arrow at a time.

original.note: Sanskrit: Lanka, Ravana's island city, built on a mountain across the sea.

trapdoor: what you thought: an action scene.
what it means: the battle outside is also a battle inside: fear and noise get in, and the hero stays level.
what a scholar hears: the Gita's sthitaprajna (2:54–72), the one whose wisdom stands still, is how many teachers read Rama in battle.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (the siege of Lanka; the night battle, roughly sargas 41–44)

notes: The night battle and the rakshasas growing stronger at night follow Valmiki as remembered; confirm the sarga and the detail of monkeys striking their own side in the dark.
Linking Rama's steadiness to the Gita's sthitaprajna is the script's own framing (with 'many teachers read'); confirm it's acceptable.
The location of Valmiki's Lanka is left unstated; many identify it with Sri Lanka, and some scholars have proposed other places.
